original_answer:
They use three evaluation metrics: Metric 1 (weighted cosine similarity), Metric 2, and Metric 3.

Metric 1 is the original metric, weighted cosine similarity, used to evaluate the final version of the results where they were ranked 5th [1]. Metric 2 was adopted after the evaluation deadline and was the basis for the first version of the results (ranked 4th) [5]. Metric 3, as presented in Cortis et al. (2017), was the basis for the second version of the results (ranked 5th) [5]. The metrics differ notably in how they penalize opposite signs between predicted and true values: Metric 2 assigns the highest error rating when signs differ, while Metric 3 penalizes opposite signs more, being otherwise similar to Metric 1 [7].

cited_sources.text: The result table 1 shows three columns based on the three evaluation metrics that the organisers have used. Metric 1 is the original metric, weighted co- sine similarity (the metric used to evaluate the ﬁnal version of the results, where we were ranked 5th; metric provided on the task website9).

This was then changed after the evaluation deadline to equa- tion 110 (which we term metric 2; this is what the ﬁrst version of the results were actually based on, where we were ranked 4th), which then changed by the organisers to their equation as presented in Cortis et al. (2017) (which we term metric 3 and what the second version of the results were based on, where we were ranked 5th).

Our systems are not optimised for this because it would predict scores of -0.01 and true value of 0.01 as very close (within vec- tor of other results) with low error whereas metric 2 would give this the highest error rating of -1 as they are not the same sign. Metric 3 is more simi- lar to metric 1 as shown by the results, however the crucial difference is that again if you get opposite signs it will penalise more.
